summary.title: Faster sorting algorithms discovered using deep reinforcement learning
summary.one_liner: AlphaDev, a deep reinforcement learning agent, found new small sorting routines at the x86 assembly level that beat human benchmarks and were merged into LLVM libc++.
keywords: monte carlo tree search program optimization
takeaways: Sorting and similar routines can be framed as a single-player game where an agent appends CPU assembly instructions and is rewarded for correctness and measured latency.
AlphaDev, an AlphaZero-based agent with a transformer representation and a dual value head for latency, found sort 3, sort 4 and sort 5 routines that are shorter or match human sorting networks.
Variable sort algorithms gained more from latency optimization, measured as the fifth percentile across 100 machines.
Discovered sequences (AlphaDev swap move and copy move) cut one instruction each from sorting-network-based code.
The sort 3/4/5 routines were reverse engineered into C++ and merged into LLVM libc++, with reported gains of up to 70% for length-five sequences and about 1.7% for very large inputs.
summary.summary: The Nature article presents AlphaDev, a deep reinforcement learning agent that treats sorting-routine design as the AssemblyGame, where it builds x86 assembly programs scored on correctness and latency. The agent is an extension of AlphaZero using Monte Carlo tree search, a transformer-based instruction encoder and a CPU state encoder. Results cover fixed sorts (3, 4, 5), variable sorts, a protobuf VarInt routine and comparisons against a stochastic superoptimization baseline. The authors report that sort 3/4/5 routines were reverse engineered into C++ and merged into LLVM libc++, with improvements measured on ARMv8, Intel Skylake and AMD Zen 2 CPUs.
